sections.h2: What do I need to know before selling a house in Mount Laurel?
sections.html:
Mount Laurel is a Burlington County township of 21.72 square miles where about 77% of homes are owner-occupied, and a sale goes through the township's Community Development office for a Certificate of Continued Occupancy, the Tax Collector for tax status, and the Burlington County Clerk for the deed.

The sections below cover the local numbers, the CCO step, quarterly tax rules, county recording costs and the choice between listing, selling yourself and accepting a cash purchase.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show for Mount Laurel?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau estimates 47,738 residents for July 1, 2025, up 7.0% from the April 2020 base. The 2020 count was 44,633, after 41,864 in 2010.

Median gross rent of $2,143 is high next to a median owned-home value of $357,200, so Mount Laurel has a visible rental market of apartments and townhouses. Retail sales of about $2.26 billion in 2022 work out to $49,149 per resident, a sign that shoppers from neighboring towns spend here.

sections.h2: How did Mount Laurel grow and what is the town like now?
sections.html:
Mount Laurel was incorporated as a township on March 7, 1872, taken from Evesham Township, and is named for a hill covered in laurel trees. It stayed a small farming community until suburban growth from Philadelphia arrived in the 1960s: the census count rose from 5,249 in 1960 to 11,221 in 1970 and 30,270 in 1990.

The township gave its name to the Mount Laurel Doctrine, the 1975 New Jersey Supreme Court ruling, reaffirmed in 1983, that requires towns to use zoning to make room for housing that low- and moderate-income households can afford. If your home carries an affordable housing deed restriction, ask the township's affordable housing office about resale rules before you list.

  • The township covers 21.99 square miles including water, and is drained by Parkers Creek and the South Branch Pennsauken Creek.
  • Ramblewood is a census-designated place of 6,655 people inside the township, and Rancocas Woods, Centerton, Hartford and Masonville are among the named localities.
  • Neighbors include Moorestown, Evesham, Medford, Lumberton, Westampton, Willingboro, Hainesport and Maple Shade, plus Cherry Hill across the county line.
  • Laurel Acres Park and part of Rancocas State Park are in the township.

sections.h2: Which roads and schools shape Mount Laurel home values?
sections.html:
Mount Laurel is built around highways. The New Jersey Turnpike crosses about 7.5 miles of the township with one exit, Exit 4 onto Route 73, and Interstate 295 has three exits here: 36, 40 and 43. Route 38, Route 73 and County Route 537 carry local traffic. NJ Transit buses 317, 413 and 457 link the township with Philadelphia and Camden.

Mount Laurel Schools cover pre-kindergarten through eighth grade: six K-4 schools (Countryside, Fleetwood, Hillside, Larchmont, Parkway and Springville) feed Hartford School for grades 5-6 and Harrington Middle School for grades 7-8. High school students attend Lenape High School in Medford, part of the Lenape Regional High School District. Because K-4 zones are geographic, a listing's attendance school is a real selling point.

sections.h2: Does Mount Laurel require a CCO when I sell?
sections.html:
Yes. Mount Laurel has a Certificate of Continued Occupancy application and checklist posted under Community Development / Construction. The township says it will not accept emailed applications, so file on paper at the municipal building at 750 Centerton Road.

Ask the Community Development office for the current fee, the timing and what must be fixed before the inspection. Handle that early: a buyer's attorney will want the certificate, and a failed item can push closing back. Landlords should also look at the township's Rental Ordinance, rental registration and safety inspection checklist, which sit on a separate Landlord Information page.

  • Pick up the application and checklist from the township's CCO page.
  • Close any open permits first.
  • Walk the checklist yourself before the inspector does.

sections.h2: When are Mount Laurel property taxes due, and what happens at closing?
sections.html:
Taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, and the grace period is 10 days under N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. The Tax Collector's page states that postmarks are not accepted and that interest is 8% on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18% above it, under N.J.S.A. 54:4-67.

The third-quarter due date moves each year. In 2026 the township had to wait for the state to set the rate, so bills went out late and the third-quarter deadline was extended to September 16, with no grace period after it. The township explains that the extended date falls 25 days after bills are mailed. Closing figures for a sale near August 1 depend on that date, so ask the Tax Collector for the amount due before the closing statement is drawn.

The Tax Collector's office at 750 Centerton Road takes payments in person, by mail, at a drop box or online. If you pay through a mortgage escrow, confirm your servicer received the bill, because a missing bill does not excuse a late payment.

sections.h2: How is a Mount Laurel deed recorded and what does Burlington County charge?
sections.html:
The Burlington County Clerk records deeds for Mount Laurel. Its page on recordable deeds sets the recording fee at $45 for the first page, with the summary sheet counted as that first page, and $10 for each added page, plus the state transfer fee based on the sale price.

A recordable deed needs the grantor and grantee names, the grantee's address, the date, the consideration, the municipal block and lot, a notarized signature and the seller's residency declaration. The clerk also noted that seller tax declarations signed on or after October 1, 2025 must use the newest state form. For sales above $1 million, the graduated percent fee under P.L. 2025, c. 69 starts at 1% of the consideration and now rests on the seller. Questions go to the County Clerk at 609-265-5122, and a free Property Fraud Alert service warns owners when a document is recorded in their name.

sections.h2: Should I list, sell myself or accept a cash offer in Mount Laurel?
sections.html:
With a median owned-home value of $357,200 and mostly owner-occupied streets, Mount Laurel suits a traditional listing when the house is in good shape. A cash purchase fits when the CCO inspection list looks long, when you are settling an estate, or when you need a firm closing date.

  • Agent listing: widest buyer pool, repairs and the CCO handled before closing.
  • For sale by owner: you pay no listing commission but handle pricing, disclosures and the contract.
  • Cash purchase: sold as-is, fewer showings, a price set for the condition you describe.

Whichever route you choose, line up the CCO, the tax status and the payoff letters first, then compare the net proceeds from each offer.

faqs.q: Do I need a certificate of continued occupancy to sell a house in Mount Laurel?
faqs.a: Yes. The township posts a CCO application and checklist on its Community Development page and does not accept emailed applications. Contact the office for fees and the inspection schedule.

faqs.q: What are the Mount Laurel tax due dates?
faqs.a: Taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a 10-day grace period. The township does not accept postmarks, so payment must arrive by the end of the grace period.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Burlington County?
faqs.a: The county lists $45 for the first page and $10 for each additional page, plus the state realty transfer fee. Sales over $1 million are also subject to the graduated percent fee for deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025.

faqs.q: Which high school serves Mount Laurel?
faqs.a: Lenape High School in Medford serves Mount Laurel students in grades 9 through 12. Mount Laurel Schools run pre-kindergarten through eighth grade.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Mount Laurel house as-is for cash?
faqs.a: Yes. An as-is sale is allowed, but the CCO inspection items and any open permits still have to be dealt with, either by you before closing or by the buyer under the contract. Ask the township what its checklist requires for your property.
